name: hook
text: Add the odd numbers, starting from one: one, three, five, and so on. The totals are one, four, nine, sixteen. Why are they always squares?

name: setup
text: Start with one dot: a one-by-one square.

name: gnomon
text: Now wrap an L-shaped border around it. Each border adds the next odd number: three, then five, then seven.

name: result
text: After n borders, the total is n squared.

name: algebra
text: Algebra agrees. Going from n minus one squared to n squared adds exactly two n minus one.

name: caveat
text: The starting point matters. Three plus five is eight, not a square. Starting from one is what makes it always work.

name: close
text: The Pythagoreans knew this gnomon trick. So every perfect square is a stack of odd numbers.
